subtopics.title: Features and Implications of Online Services

items.definition: Buying and selling goods and services online, with ordering, payment and delivery handled digitally.
items.examples: Amazon; ASOS; Tesco online groceries.
items.examTip: Cover both sides: convenience for customers AND the decline of the high street.
keyFacts: Customers get 24/7 shopping, more choice and easy price comparison, so they can find the best deal
Retailers get lower costs and global reach, because they need fewer shops and can sell anywhere
Risks include fraud, data breaches and not being able to inspect items before buying
Society sees high-street closures but more warehouse and delivery jobs

items.definition: Banking, insurance and payments done online without visiting a branch.
items.examples: Banking apps; PayPal; Monzo.
items.examTip: Benefits: 24/7, instant transfers. Risks: fraud, phishing, excluding less digital customers.
keyFacts: Check balances, pay and transfer any time, so customers don't need to visit a branch
Near-instant payments, so money reaches people and businesses straight away
App-only banks have lower costs, because they don't run branches, so they can offer better rates
Elderly or offline customers can be excluded as branches close

items.definition: Courses, lessons and qualifications delivered over the internet.
items.examples: Google Classroom; BBC Bitesize; Coursera.
items.examTip: Benefits: anywhere, self-paced, cheaper. Drawbacks: needs internet, less contact, self-discipline.
keyFacts: VLEs hold resources, homework and feedback, so learners can study and catch up anywhere
Reaches rural and remote learners who can't easily travel to a college
Learners without devices are disadvantaged, widening the digital divide
Less face-to-face interaction, so some learners feel isolated or lose motivation

items.definition: News and information delivered through websites, apps and social media.
items.examples: BBC News online; Wikipedia; news on X.
items.examTip: Key issues: fake news, filter bubbles, speed vs accuracy.
keyFacts: Published within minutes, so people hear about events as they happen
Anyone can publish, so misinformation spreads quickly
Filter bubbles show only agreeable views, because algorithms recommend what users already like
Paywalls replace print advertising, because newspapers need a new way to earn money

items.definition: Music, films, TV and games delivered on demand over the internet.
items.examples: Netflix; Spotify; Steam.
items.examTip: Streaming has disrupted DVDs, CDs and broadcast TV. Watch for piracy and age checks.
keyFacts: Streaming needs internet, but downloads work offline, e.g. for watching on a flight
Subscriptions replaced buying, so users get large libraries for a monthly fee but own nothing
4K streaming needs about 25 Mbps, so homes with slow broadband get lower quality
Piracy breaks copyright law and takes income away from creators

items.definition: Systems that let customers check availability, reserve and pay online in real time.
items.examples: Booking.com; Trainline; NHS GP appointments.
items.examTip: Benefits: 24/7, instant confirmation, less admin. Risks: double booking, downtime, data security.
keyFacts: Live availability and instant confirmation, so customers know straight away that they're booked
Bookings outside opening hours, so the business takes bookings without staff on duty
Must sync with internal systems or it will double-book the same slot
Collects personal and payment data, so it must be kept secure under GDPR

comparisonTable.title: Online Services: Benefits and Risks by Sector

Phishing fraud, financial exclusion of elderly
Digital divide, lack of interaction, self-discipline needed
Piracy, addiction design, age verification gaps

subtopics.title: Uses, Impact and Implications of IT for Individuals and Organisations

items.definition: Data recorded when a customer interacts with an organisation: what, when, how much, how paid.
items.examples: Supermarket till records; bank card transactions; order history.
items.examTip: Raw data becomes valuable once analysed. Link to targeted marketing and stock control.
keyFacts: Used for forecasting and restocking, so shops hold the right stock at the right time
Powers recommendations and targeted adverts, which increase sales
Loyalty cards link it to named people, so the organisation learns each customer's habits
Must be stored securely under GDPR, because it is personal data

items.definition: Using data about a person's behaviour to show them personalised adverts.
items.examples: Amazon recommendations; adverts that follow you across websites.
items.examTip: Businesses get more sales; users get relevant ads. But privacy and consent are concerns.
keyFacts: Uses cookies, purchase and browsing history to work out what each person is interested in
Cheaper and more effective than blanket adverts, because adverts only reach likely buyers
Can feel intrusive, so some customers are put off when adverts seem to know too much
GDPR requires cookie consent and an opt-out, so users can refuse tracking

items.definition: IT tools that let people work on the same files and projects at once from anywhere.
items.examples: Google Docs; Microsoft Teams; Trello.
items.examTip: Link to productivity, remote working and always-on work culture.
keyFacts: Several people edit at once, so work is finished faster without emailing copies around
Version history tracks changes, so mistakes can be undone and everyone sees who changed what
Chat, video and files in one place, so teams don't switch between tools
Needs internet and can blur work and home, because staff can be reached at any time

items.definition: Working away from the office using VPNs, cloud apps and video calls.
items.examples: Staff working from home over a VPN.
items.examTip: Link the technology (VPN, cloud, collaboration tools) to impacts on the business and staff.
keyFacts: Organisation needs less office space and can hire from a wider talent pool, not just locally
Staff save the commute and get flexible hours, which can improve work-life balance
Risks include insecure home networks, and teams are harder to manage when no one is in the office
Staff risk isolation and blurred boundaries, because home becomes the workplace

rows: Raw records of customer interactions (purchases, clicks, payments)
Using customer data to personalise advertising and recommendations

Operational record-keeping, stock management, demand forecasting
Increase sales conversions, improve customer experience
POS systems, website analytics, payment records
Transactional data + browsing history + demographics + social media
Informs stock ordering, identifies best-sellers, detects fraud
Higher conversion rate; more cost-effective than mass advertising
Enables faster checkout, loyalty rewards, personalised receipts
Relevant product suggestions; less irrelevant advertising
Individual purchases linked to named persons — GDPR applies
Tracking across websites; consent often unclear; feels intrusive
Store securely, use only for stated purpose, retain no longer than necessary
Explicit cookie consent; right to opt out of tracking

items.definition: New data collected first-hand for a specific current purpose.
items.examples: A customer satisfaction survey; running a focus group.
items.examTip: Collected by you, for your purpose, now. Relevant but slow and costly.
keyFacts: Exactly fits your needs, because you choose the questions and who to ask
Up to date, because it is collected now for this purpose
Methods include surveys, interviews, focus groups and observation, chosen to suit the question
Expensive and time-consuming, because the data has to be gathered from scratch

items.definition: Data that already exists, collected by someone else for another purpose.
items.examples: Census data; published market research.
items.examTip: Collected by someone else, earlier. Cheap and quick, but may be out of date or not fit.
keyFacts: No collection needed, because the data already exists in reports, databases or websites
Cheaper and quicker than primary data, so it suits early research
May be outdated or not fit your needs, because it was collected for another purpose
Check how credible the source is, because you don't control how it was collected

Highly specific to exact research needs

Full control over how data is collected
No control — must trust original methodology
Census data, industry reports, published research

subtopics.title: Methods of Ensuring Reliability of Information

items.term: Methods of Ensuring Reliability of Information
items.definition: Checking information is trustworthy and consistent before relying on it.
items.examples: Checking a story against several reputable sources.
items.examTip: Say how an organisation checks information before using it to make decisions.
keyFacts: Cross-reference several independent sources, so one wrong source doesn't mislead you
Check the author, date and publisher, so you know the information is current and from an expert
Prefer peer-reviewed or official sources, because experts have checked them
Compare with past data to spot anomalies, so unusual figures are questioned before being used

subtopics.title: Methods of Collecting Data and Opinions

items.definition: Structured questions sent to many people to gather measurable data.
items.examples: An email survey after a purchase.
items.examTip: Best for large numbers and statistics. Watch for bias in who replies.
keyFacts: Online surveys are cheap and fast, so they reach many people with little effort
Closed questions are easy to analyse, because answers can be counted and graphed
Response rates are often low, so results may not represent everyone
Leading questions skew results, because they push people towards a particular answer

items.definition: A fixed set of written questions, on paper or online.
items.examples: A feedback form handed to shoppers.
items.examTip: Very close to a survey: the questionnaire is the document itself.
keyFacts: Cheap to send to many people, by post or online
Rating scales measure opinions, so feelings can be turned into numbers and compared
Cannot follow up answers, so unclear or interesting replies can't be explored
Low response rates, because many people ignore questionnaires

items.definition: A small group (6–10) discussing a topic in depth, led by a facilitator.
items.examples: Testing a prototype app with potential users.
items.examTip: Shows WHY people think something; surveys show HOW MANY.
keyFacts: Rich, detailed opinions, because people discuss and build on each other's ideas
Facilitator can follow up, so interesting points can be explored further
Expensive to run, because of venue, facilitator and participants' time
Strong personalities can sway the group, so quieter views may be lost

items.definition: A one-to-one conversation to gather detailed views and experiences.
items.examples: Interviewing customers about a new product.
items.examTip: Structured = fixed questions; unstructured = flexible conversation.
keyFacts: Can probe and ask follow-ups, so the interviewer gets detailed, in-depth answers
Time-consuming, so only small samples are possible
Interviewer can influence answers through tone or wording, which biases results

comparisonTable.title: Data Collection Methods Compared
rows: Low response rates; no depth; bias possible
Rich discussion; reveals WHY; unexpected insights
Not representative; group dynamics; small sample
Expensive; interviewer bias; small sample; hard to generalise

items.definition: Data must be correct and complete, because bad data leads to bad decisions and legal problems.
items.examples: A hospital giving the wrong drug because of an incorrect record.
items.examTip: Give a specific consequence from the scenario.
keyFacts: GDPR requires accurate personal data, so inaccurate records break the law
Wrong data leads to wrong decisions, e.g. targeting the wrong customers
Errors damage customer trust, e.g. wrong bills or orders sent to the wrong address
Wrong stock data leads to over- or under-ordering, wasting money or losing sales

items.definition: Checking data was copied correctly, e.g. by entering it twice or proofreading.
items.examples: Typing a password twice to confirm it.
items.examTip: Checks it was copied correctly, not that it is actually right.
keyFacts: Double entry: data is typed twice and must match, so a typing slip is spotted
Proofreading against the original, so the copy matches the source document
Catches typing mistakes only, because it can't tell if the original data was wrong

items.definition: Automatic checks that data is sensible and follows rules before it is accepted.
items.examples: Rejecting an age of 200; a required email field.
items.examTip: Know the checks: range, presence, format, length, type, lookup.
keyFacts: Range check keeps values within limits, e.g. an age between 0 and 120
Presence check stops a field being left empty, so required data is always entered
Format check matches a pattern (e.g. postcode), so data is entered in the right shape
Type and length checks stop text in number fields and over-long entries
Valid data can still be wrong, because a sensible-looking value may still be incorrect

comparisonTable.title: Verification vs Validation
rows: Whether data was entered the same as the source
Whether data is reasonable, complete, correct format
When data is submitted to the system
Out-of-range values, missing fields, wrong format/type
Whether the original data itself is correct
Whether the data is actually true (just whether it's plausible)
Password typed same way twice — PASS. Different — FAIL.
Age entered as 250 — FAIL range check. Age 25 — PASS.
Range, presence, format, length, type, lookup checks
Always automated — built into the system

subtopics.title: User Interface Characteristics for Data Collection Systems

items.definition: How easily users can find their way around and enter data without training.
items.examTip: Easy interfaces mean fewer errors and faster entry.
keyFacts: Fields in a logical order, so users fill the form in naturally without jumping around
Clear labels, so users know exactly what to enter in each field
Drop-downs and autocomplete reduce typing, which saves time and cuts errors

items.definition: Designing interfaces so people with disabilities can use them.
items.examTip: An ethical and legal duty (Equality Act 2010). Link to assistive technology.
keyFacts: Works with screen readers, so blind and partially sighted users can use it
Strong colour contrast, so text is readable for people with visual impairments
Usable by keyboard alone, so people who can't use a mouse aren't excluded
Works when text is enlarged, so users who need bigger text can still use every feature

items.definition: Design features that stop users entering wrong data in the first place.
items.examTip: Preventing errors beats catching them afterwards.
keyFacts: Error messages as you type, so mistakes are fixed straight away
Date pickers and drop-downs limit input, so users can only choose valid options
Messages say how to fix the error, so users aren't left guessing
'Are you sure?' before irreversible actions, so data isn't deleted by accident

items.definition: Whether the interface has every feature users need to complete their tasks.
items.examTip: Too few features block tasks; too many confuse users.
keyFacts: All required fields present, so users can complete the task without workarounds
Search to avoid duplicate records, so the same customer isn't entered twice
Links to other systems to avoid re-typing, which saves time and cuts errors

items.definition: How quickly the interface responds, including at busy times.
items.examTip: Slow interfaces make users rush and make mistakes.
keyFacts: Slow pages make users give up, so the organisation loses customers or sales
Must cope with peak use, so it doesn't slow down or crash when busiest
Show progress for long tasks, so users know it is still working and don't give up

items.definition: Whether the interface works on all devices, browsers and screen sizes.
items.examTip: Compatibility = works everywhere, including phones and assistive technology.
keyFacts: Works in all major browsers, so no user is locked out by their choice of browser
Works on Windows, macOS, Android and iOS, so it reaches users on any device
Responsive design fits every screen size, so it is usable on phones as well as PCs
